✦ The Secret in the Squares ✦

Pythagoras, a clay tablet a thousand years older than he was, and the theorem that has been proved some 370 different ways

Nobody knows what Pythagoras looked like. What you are looking at is what later centuries thought a wise man ought to look like: a portrait of a reputation.

Chapter One · Samos and Croton · about 570–495 BC

The Man Behind the Curtain

Around 530 BC, a ship from the Greek island of Samos docked at Croton, a rich port near the toe of Italy's boot. Off stepped a man named Pythagoras. Within a few years he was the most talked-about person in the city, and the leader of something the world had not seen before: part school, part secret society. His followers shared their belongings, lived by his rules, and kept his teachings to themselves. New members, the old stories say, spent their first years in silence, listening to the master speak from behind a curtain. They were allowed to hear him, but not to see him.

Members were expected to adhere to strict rules Never eat beans. Never stir a fire with a knife. Don't pick up what has fallen from the table. When you get out of bed, smooth the sheets so your body leaves no print. Don't let swallows nest under your roof. Nobody is sure what the rules were for. His critics were already arguing about the beans. But the Pythagoreans kept to the rules without question.

They also believed that souls are born again, into new people and into animals. A poet named Xenophanes, who was alive at the same time, made a joke of it: Pythagoras sees a man beating a puppy and cries out to stop, because that's the soul of a friend, and he recognized the voice!

Because here is the trouble with Pythagoras. He left no writings. Not one line in his own words survives. His followers were sworn to secrecy, and they had a habit of crediting every discovery to the master; their way of ending an argument was "He himself said it." The detailed biographies we have were written seven or eight hundred years after he died, by admirers, and they are stuffed with wonders: a thigh made of gold, a river that greeted him by name, a day when he was seen in two cities at once. So all through this lesson, watch for three little words: the story goes. When you see them, a legend is coming, and your job is to ask how anybody could know.

And behind the curtain, they did geometry. Later Greek writers credit the Pythagoreans with one of the first facts every geometry student learns: the three angles of any triangle, added together, always make exactly two square corners, or 180 degrees. Fat triangle, thin triangle, it makes no difference. You can test it with scissors: tear the three corners off a paper triangle, lay them point to point, and they line up along a straight edge every time.

🫘 Even his death comes in three versions. In one, enemies chase him to the edge of a bean field; he refuses to trample the beans, and is caught. In another he starves in a temple. In a third he simply dies, old, in the town of Metapontum. The ancient writers who tell these stories tell all of them, which shows you how much anyone really knew.

A woodcut from Franchino Gaffurio's Theorica musicae, printed in Milan in 1492. Read the labels. Three panels say PYTAGORA or PITAGORAS: he strikes bells, taps glasses of water, plucks strings stretched by weights, and tries pipes with a partner labelled PHYLOLAUS. Everything carries the same numbers: 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16. But the forge, top left, is labelled IUBAL: Jubal, the Bible's first musician. By 1492 the hammer story had been told so often that it had two heroes. And here is the catch: apart from the pipes, none of these experiments works as drawn. Weights in those ratios do not tune strings to those notes. For two thousand years it was easier to copy the picture than to pick up a hammer.

The Lute Player, painted by Caravaggio in Rome around 1596 and now in the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg. This is the instrument Vincenzo Galilei played and wrote books about. Look at how the head of the lute bends sharply backwards, with a row of pegs down each side. The strings run in pairs, and each pair is tuned by stretching it tighter or looser with its peg. That is why a lute player was the right person to ask how much pull it takes to raise a string by an octave: he did it by hand every time he tuned up.

Chapter Two · Croton · about 520 BC

All Is Number

What did the brotherhood actually study behind that curtain? Numbers, but not the way a shopkeeper studies them. The Pythagoreans had noticed something that stunned them, and it came out of music.

Stretch a string tight and pluck it: you get a note. Now press the string down at exactly its halfway point and pluck again. The new note is higher, yet somehow it is the same note, the jump musicians call an octave. Let two-thirds of the string sound instead, and you get the strong, sweet jump called a fifth. Let three-quarters sound, and you get a fourth. The notes that belong together come from the simplest fractions there are: 1/2, 2/3, 3/4. Press just anywhere, and mostly you get mud.

Your monochord · one string, one movable bridge
Click the string above any mark, and listen.
Each click plays the whole string, then the shortened string, then both together. Turn your sound on.

Think about how strange that is. Your ear, which has never heard of fractions, can tell a two-thirds string from a clumsy one. Beauty was obeying arithmetic. The Pythagoreans drew the wildest conclusion they could: if number rules music, maybe number rules everything: the planets, the seasons, the world itself. Their creed comes down to us as "All is number." It was a guess, and an enormous one. It is also, more or less, the guess that all of physics has been built on ever since.

Their holiest symbol was a triangle of ten dots called the tetractys (tet-RAK-tiss): rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4. Look at neighbouring rows and you'll find the music hiding inside: 2 to 1, 3 to 2, 4 to 3. Pythagoreans swore their oaths by it.

The story goes that Pythagoras found the musical ratios while walking past a blacksmith's forge: he heard the hammers ringing in harmony, weighed them, and found their weights stood in the ratios 12, 9, 8 and 6. It is a wonderful story, and it was copied from book to book for more than a thousand years. It is also false, and anyone with two hammers could have found that out. A hammer twice as heavy does not ring an octave lower. Nobody checked; they trusted the book. When an Italian lute player named Vincenzo Galilei finally hung real weights on real strings in the 1580s, he found the old numbers wrong there too: to raise a string one octave you need four times the weight, not two. (His son Galileo picked up the habit of checking.)

The string lengths, though, are true. And unlike the scholars who copied the hammer story, you have just tested them with your own ears.

🌟 Big Idea #1: A story can be repeated for a thousand years and still be wrong. What made the string ratios knowledge and the hammers a legend was not who told them or how often. It was that one of them survives being tested.
★ Checkpoint 3 · Tune the string
The monochord's rule works on any string. A harp string is 90 cm long. To sound the fifth above its note, exactly two-thirds of it must vibrate. How many centimeters is that?
cm
One third of 90 is 30. Two thirds is twice that.
★ Checkpoint 4 · Grow the tetractys
The tetractys has rows of 1, 2, 3 and 4 dots, ten in all. Add one more row underneath, with 5 dots. How many dots does the bigger triangle have?
dots
1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. (Numbers you can stack into triangles like this are called triangular numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The Pythagoreans loved them.)
Chapter Three · The theorem itself

The Secret in the Squares

Now for the thing with his name on it. Start with a right triangle: a triangle with one perfectly square corner, like the corner of this page. The two sides that make the square corner are the legs. The third side, the long slanting one across from the corner, is the hypotenuse (hy-POT-en-ooss), from Greek words meaning "stretched underneath."

Here is the secret. Build a square on each of the three sides, like three square fields, each fenced along one edge of the triangle. Then, for every right triangle that ever was or ever will be:

📐 The Pythagorean Theorem: the square on one leg plus the square on the other leg equals the square on the hypotenuse. With legs a and b and hypotenuse c, that is: a² + b² = c².

(The little raised 2 is read "squared." a² means a × a, the area of a square whose side is a. That is exactly why multiplying a number by itself is called squaring it.)

Try the most famous triangle of all, with legs 3 and 4. The squares on the legs hold 9 and 16 little unit squares. (Count them in the machine below.) Together that makes 25. And 25 is 5 × 5, so the hypotenuse is exactly 5. Notice what just happened: nobody measured that slanting side. We calculated it from the other two. That is the whole power of the theorem: know two sides of a right triangle, and the third can't hide from you.

Your theorem machine · build any right triangle
a² = 9 b² = 16 a² + b² = 25
 

Drag the sliders for a while and you'll notice something. Most triangles give a messy hypotenuse. Legs 4 and 5 make a square of 41, and no whole number times itself is 41. Whole-number triangles like 3-4-5 are rare treasures. They have a name: Pythagorean triples. Hold on to the word "rare." It matters in the next chapter.

★ Checkpoint 5 · Count the squares
A right triangle has legs 3 and 4. The squares on its legs have areas 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16. What is the area of the square on its hypotenuse?
unit squares
The theorem says: just add the two smaller squares. 9 + 16.

Now one on your own. The legs are 6 and 8. How long is the hypotenuse? (Square each leg, add, then ask: what number times itself gives that?)
units
6 × 6 = 36 and 8 × 8 = 64. Together, 100. What times itself is 100?

Set your theorem machine to legs 5 and 12, or work it by hand. How long is the hypotenuse?
units

Plimpton 322, now at Columbia University in New York: clay, about 13 centimeters wide, written around 1800 BC. The scribe ruled it into columns with a straight edge (you can still see the lines) and filled fifteen rows with numbers in base 60, pressed in with the corner of a reed. The left edge is broken off, and traces of glue suggest the missing piece was lost in modern times. Scholars still argue about what it was for. One strong suggestion: a teacher's list, for setting right-triangle problems that were certain to come out in whole numbers.
Plimpton 322, Babylon, about 1800 BC · hover to unroll · click to enlarge
YBC 7289, in the Yale Babylonian Collection, about 8 centimeters across, small enough to sit in a palm, and round like the practice tablets Babylonian students used. The square is drawn tilted, standing on one corner, with both diagonals. Near the top-left edge are three wedges: 30, the length of the side. Along the level diagonal run the numbers 1, 24, 51, 10, the square root of 2 in base 60, and beneath them 42, 25, 35: the diagonal itself, 30 times as long. A value that good was not worked out on the spot: it was copied from a table, the way you might look a number up today.

Chapter Four · Babylon, India, China · from 1800 BC

A Thousand Years Too Early

After all that, here is a fact that may come as a shock: Pythagoras did not discover the Pythagorean theorem. He wasn't even close to first.

Around 1922 a New York publisher named George Plimpton bought a broken clay tablet, smaller than a postcard, from a dealer in antiquities. The price is said to have been about ten dollars. It had been written in what is now southern Iraq around 1800 BC, in wedge-shaped cuneiform pressed into wet clay with a cut reed. Scholars call it Plimpton 322. When its numbers were finally worked out in 1945, the tablet turned out to be a table: fifteen rows, and every row belongs to a right triangle with whole-number sides. Not just baby ones like 3-4-5. One row gives 119, 120, 169. Another gives 12,709, 13,500, 18,541. You just learned how rare such triples are. Nobody stumbles on fifteen of them by luck. Whoever wrote that tablet knew the rule, and knew it cold.

A second tablet from about the same age, small and round, the kind a student held in one palm, shows a square with its diagonals scratched in, and along the diagonal a string of numbers. They give the diagonal's length correct to better than one part in a million. It looks very much like somebody's homework.

And Babylon was not alone. In India, the Sulba Sutras ("the rules of the cord") were handbooks for laying out altars with stretched ropes. The oldest goes under the name of Baudhayana, was composed perhaps between 800 and 500 BC, and says it plainly: the rope stretched along the diagonal of a rectangle makes an area equal to what the two sides make together. In China, an old book of astronomy and mathematics called the Zhoubi Suanjing works the 3-4-5 triangle as a conversation between a duke and a wise man. The Chinese names for the three sides are gou, gu and xian, meaning "hook," "thigh" and "bowstring," and Chinese students today learn the rule as the gougu theorem. Pythagoras's name isn't on it at all.

So why do we call it Pythagoras's? Because the Greeks who came after him gave him, or his school, the credit for something new. Not the rule. The proof. A Babylonian scribe had a recipe that worked every time anyone tried it. But "it has always worked" and "it cannot ever fail" are two different claims, and the space between them is the whole of mathematics. A proof is an argument so airtight that it covers every right triangle at once: the big ones, the skinny ones, the ones nobody has drawn yet.

And now the honest part. We have no proof in Pythagoras's own hand, and no writer from his own century says he made one. The story goes that when he found it, he sacrificed an ox to the gods. In some versions it was a hundred oxen. A man whose followers believed animals carried the souls of their friends? Even ancient writers raised an eyebrow at that. What we can say is this: by the time the Greeks wrote their mathematics down, the proof was there. The next four chapters will show you five of them.

🪢 You may read that Egyptian builders made their square corners with a rope knotted into 12 equal parts, pulled tight into a 3-4-5 triangle. The trick really works, and carpenters still use it. But no Egyptian text or picture shows anyone doing it. A historian suggested the idea in the 1800s as a guess, and it has been repeated ever since until it sounds like a fact. It might even be true. It just isn't known.
🌟 Big Idea #2: A rule that has worked every time is evidence. A proof is a different kind of thing: it rules out the exception before anyone goes looking for it. Evidence says "so far." Proof says "always."
★ Checkpoint 8 · How late was Pythagoras?
Plimpton 322 was written about 1800 BC. Pythagoras was born about 570 BC. How many years before his birth was the tablet already sitting in Babylon?
years
Both dates are BC, so just subtract: 1800 − 570.
★ Checkpoint 9 · Read a row of the tablet
One row of Plimpton 322 belongs to a triangle with legs 45 and 60. The scribe's squares would be 45 × 45 = 2,025 and 60 × 60 = 3,600. How long is the hypotenuse the tablet records?
units
2,025 + 3,600 = 5,625. Now hunt for the number that squares to 5,625: 70 × 70 is 4,900 and 80 × 80 is 6,400, and the answer must end in 5. (Divide all three sides by 15 and see which old friend appears.)
★ Checkpoint 10 · What was left to do?
Babylonian scribes were using the rule more than a thousand years before the Greeks. So what did the Greeks add that was truly new?
Chapter Five · Proof One · older than its own history

The Sliding Triangles

Here is the first proof, and many people think it is the most beautiful. Nobody knows who saw it first. Some historians guess that it is the kind of proof the early Pythagoreans would have used, scratched in sand; pictures like it turn up in China and India too. It needs no algebra and almost no words.

Cut out four copies of the same right triangle. Any right triangle will do; call its legs a and b. Make a square tray just big enough that one a and one b fit along each side. Now lay the four triangles in the four corners, each turned a quarter-turn from the last.

Look at the empty space in the middle. Every one of its four sides is a hypotenuse, so all four sides have length c. And its corners are true square corners. (Where two triangles meet on the tray's edge, three angles share one straight line: a sharp angle from each triangle, and the corner of the hole between them. A straight line is worth two square corners. The two sharp angles of a right triangle always add up to one. So the hole's corner gets the other.) So the hole is a tilted square with side c. Its area is c².

Below are two copies of that tray. Press the button and watch the triangles in the right-hand one slide. The left-hand one stays put, so you can compare.

The sliding proof · four triangles in a square tray
Before: one tilted square, side c
The same tray, the same triangles
long and thinthe tray stays 7 × 7long and thin

The triangles pair up into two rectangles, and the empty space becomes two squares: one with side a, one with side b. But nothing was added and nothing was taken away. It is the same tray. They are the same four triangles. So the empty space must be exactly as big as it was before:

📐 empty space before = empty space after, so  c² = a² + b².  That's the whole proof.

Now drag the slider and change the triangle. Make it fat, thin, nearly flat, and slide them again. It works every time, and you can see that it has to.

★ Checkpoint 11 · Check it with numbers
Use the 3-4-5 triangle. The tray is 7 × 7, so its area is 49. Each triangle has area 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6, and there are four of them. How much empty space is left in the tray?
unit squares
Four triangles cover 4 × 6 = 24. Take that from 49. (And notice: 25 is both 5 × 5 and 9 + 16.)
★ Checkpoint 12 · Why is this a proof, and not just another example?
You checked the tray with a 3-4-5 triangle. Why does the sliding argument settle the question for every right triangle?
The xian tu as printed in a later edition of the Zhoubi Suanjing. Count the grid: it is 7 by 7, and the tilted square inside it is the square on the hypotenuse of a 3-4-5 triangle. The column of writing on the left reads, roughly: “the squares on gou and gu, joined together, make the square on xian.” The labels inside follow Zhao Shuang's instructions: 朱 (zhu, red) on the triangles, 黃 (huang, yellow) on the little square in the middle. Chapter Six · Proof Two · China · written down by the 200s AD

The Bowstring Diagram

The Zhoubi Suanjing took the shape we know roughly two thousand years ago, from material that was older. In the 200s AD a scholar named Zhao Shuang wrote a commentary on it, and into that commentary he put a picture: the xian tu, the "bowstring diagram." His notes even say what colours to paint it: the triangles red, the little square in the middle yellow.

This time, start with the big square, the one on the hypotenuse with side c, and fill it up. Four copies of the triangle fit inside like the blades of a pinwheel, each with its hypotenuse lying along one side of the square. They don't quite fill it. In the very middle a small square is left over, and its side is the difference between the two legs: b − a.

For the 3-4-5 triangle, each red triangle has area 6, and the yellow square has side 4 − 3 = 1, so its area is 1. Add it all up: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 1 = 25. And 25 is exactly 9 + 16. With a little algebra (which you will meet in a few years) the same sum can be done with plain a and b in place of the numbers, and it comes out to a² + b² for every right triangle there is.

Put the two proofs side by side. In the last chapter the triangles sat outside the tilted square. Here they sit inside it. It is the same idea, seen from the other side of the world.

📜 The same picture appears in India around AD 1150, in the work of the great mathematician Bhaskara. The story goes that he drew the figure and wrote beside it one single word of proof: "Behold!" It's a marvellous story, told in many books. But historians who have gone looking for that word in what Bhaskara actually wrote have come back without it. He explained his figure with a calculation, like everybody else.
★ Checkpoint 13 · Fill a bigger square
Try the bowstring diagram on the 5-12-13 triangle. Each triangle has area 5 × 12 ÷ 2 = 30, and there are four. The little middle square has side 12 − 5 = 7, so its area is 49. What is the area of the whole big square?
unit squares
4 × 30 = 120, plus the 49 in the middle. (Then check: is your answer 13 × 13? Is it 25 + 144?)
Two pages of Vatican manuscript Greek 190, written out by hand in the 800s or 900s AD, one of the oldest complete copies of Euclid's Elements on Earth. Find the windmill in the middle of the right-hand page. Then look in the margins and along the bottom: later readers, over centuries, squeezed in their own notes and their own little diagrams. Nothing in Euclid's handwriting survives; this copy was made more than a thousand years after he died. The proof survived by being copied, scribe after scribe, and because any reader, at any time, could check every step without taking anybody's word for it.

Chapter Seven · Proof Three · Alexandria · about 300 BC

Euclid's Windmill

Around 300 BC, in the new city of Alexandria in Egypt, a teacher named Euclid wrote the most successful textbook of all time. The Elements starts from a handful of statements so plain that nobody could doubt them, such as you can draw a straight line between any two points. Then it builds, step by locked step, each new result resting only on the ones before it. It was still being used in schoolrooms more than two thousand years later.

The first of its thirteen books climbs through forty-six propositions like a staircase. At the top stands Proposition 47: the theorem of Pythagoras. Generations of students gave its diagram nicknames: the windmill, the bride's chair, the peacock's tail.

Euclid's idea is different from the sliding proofs, and cleverer. He drops a line from the square corner straight down through the big square, slicing it into two rectangles. Then, using triangles that he slides and turns without changing their area, he proves that the left rectangle is exactly as big as the square on the left leg, and the right rectangle exactly as big as the square on the right leg.

So the two small squares don't merely add up to the big one. Each has its own place inside it. Euclid shows you where the 9 goes, and where the 16 goes.

His very next proposition, number 48, runs the theorem backwards: if a triangle's sides obey a² + b² = c², then it must have a square corner. That is what makes the carpenter's knotted rope work. And there the first book ends.

😲 Around 1629, an Englishman named Thomas Hobbes, forty years old and no mathematician, saw a copy of Euclid lying open in a library at Proposition 47. He read the claim and said out loud, with a swear word, "This is impossible!" So he read the proof. It sent him back to an earlier proposition, which sent him back to another, and another, all the way to the beginning, until he was convinced. His friend John Aubrey, who wrote the story down, says: "This made him in love with geometry."
★ Checkpoint 14 · Where does the 9 go?
In the windmill for the 3-4-5 triangle, the big square is 5 tall. Euclid's line cuts off a rectangle on the left that is 1.8 wide and 5 tall. What is its area, and which square does that match?
unit squares
1.8 × 5. Think of it as 18 × 5 = 90, then put the decimal point back. (The other rectangle is 3.2 × 5 = 16. There are your two squares.)

Born in a log cabin in Ohio in 1831, he worked his way through school, taught Greek and Latin, and was running a college at twenty-six. His trapezoid proof was printed on April 1, 1876, while he sat in Congress. He became President in March 1881, was shot by an assassin that July, and died in September, two hundred days after taking office. The proof has lasted rather longer.

Chapter Eight · Proofs Four and Five · 1876 and about 1891

The Congressman and the Schoolboy

You don't have to be a mathematician to prove the theorem. You have to be stubborn, and you have to like it.

James A. Garfield had been a schoolteacher and the head of a small Ohio college before he became a general in the Civil War and then a congressman. In 1876, passing the time with other members of Congress, he found a proof of his own. It was printed that April in the New-England Journal of Education. Five years later he was sworn in as the twentieth President of the United States. He is the only one, so far, to have published a proof of the Pythagorean theorem.

Garfield's trick is to stand two copies of the triangle on one straight line, toe to toe, and join their tops. The shape you get is a trapezoid, a four-sided figure with two parallel sides, and it is made of exactly three triangles: the two copies, and between them a big one with two sides of length c and a square corner. That middle triangle is half of a square with side c.

Now measure the trapezoid two ways. As one whole shape, its area is the average of its two parallel sides, times the distance between them. As three pieces, its area is triangle + triangle + half of c². The two answers must agree, and out falls the theorem. You'll run the numbers yourself below.

The fifth proof belongs to a boy. In Munich, around 1891, an engineer named Jakob Einstein told his nephew Albert, who was eleven or twelve, about the theorem of Pythagoras. Albert did not look the proof up. He decided to find one. Many years later he remembered: "After much effort I succeeded in 'proving' this theorem on the basis of the similarity of triangles."

Similar triangles are triangles with the same shape in different sizes: scale models of each other. We don't have the boy's notebook, so nobody can say exactly which steps he took. But here is a proof of just the kind he describes. Drop a line from the square corner straight to the hypotenuse:

The triangle splits into two smaller ones, and both are scale models of the whole, with the same angles and the same shape. Look at their longest sides. The blue one's hypotenuse is the old leg a. The gold one's is the old leg b. The whole triangle's is c.

Now a fact about scale models: area grows as the square of the size. Double every length and the area is four times as big; triple them and it is nine times. So for triangles of this one shape, the area is always the same fixed fraction of the square on the hypotenuse. For the 3-4-5 shape that fraction happens to be 0.24: the whole triangle has area 0.24 × 25 = 6.

So the three areas are 0.24 × a², 0.24 × b² and 0.24 × c². But the two small triangles are the big one, cut in two. Their areas add up to its area. Divide away the 0.24, and what is left says a² + b² = c². No squares were drawn at all.

🌟 Big Idea #3: Nobody asked Garfield for a proof, and the theorem had been settled for two thousand years when Einstein's uncle mentioned it. They proved it anyway, because being told something is true and seeing for yourself why are not the same experience.
★ Checkpoint 15 · Garfield's trapezoid, measured whole
For the 3-4-5 triangle, the trapezoid's two parallel sides are 3 and 4 long, and they stand 7 apart. Area of a trapezoid = (average of the parallel sides) × (distance between them). What is the area?
unit squares
The average of 3 and 4 is 3.5. Then 3.5 × 7.
★ Checkpoint 16 · Garfield's trapezoid, measured in pieces
The whole trapezoid is 24.5. Take away the two triangles, which have area 6 each. What remains is half of the square on the hypotenuse. So what is the area of the whole square on the hypotenuse?
unit squares
24.5 − 6 − 6 = 12.5. That is half of c². Double it.
★ Checkpoint 17 · The schoolboy's proof, checked
In the 3-4-5 shape, a triangle's area is always 0.24 × the square on its hypotenuse. The small blue triangle has area 0.24 × 9 = 2.16. The gold one has area 0.24 × 16 = 3.84. Add them. What do you get?
unit squares
2.16 + 3.84. (And the whole 3-4-5 triangle's area is 3 × 4 ÷ 2. The pieces make the whole. That was the entire proof.)
Chapter Nine · Southern Italy · the 400s BC

The Number That Would Not Behave

Remember the creed: All is number. By "number" the Pythagoreans meant whole numbers (1, 2, 3) and the ratios between them, like 3/2 or 17/12. Every length in the world, they believed, could be written as one of those. And then their own theorem turned on them.

Take the simplest right triangle there is: both legs exactly 1. It is half of a square, cut corner to corner.

The theorem says c² = 1 + 1 = 2. So the diagonal is whatever number, multiplied by itself, makes 2. We call it the square root of 2 and write it √2. Fine. Which fraction is it?

Try 7/5, which is 1.4. Squared, it falls a little short of 2. Try 17/12: squared, it lands a hair the other side. Try 41/29, try 99/70: closer, and closer, and never there. Look at how they miss. For a fraction to equal √2, the top number squared would have to be exactly double the bottom number squared:

7 × 7 = 49  but  2 × 5 × 5 = 50
17 × 17 = ?  but  2 × 12 × 12 = 288  (that one is yours, below)
41 × 41 = 1,681  but  2 × 29 × 29 = 1,682
99 × 99 = 9,801  but  2 × 70 × 70 = 9,800

Off by one. Every time. The Greeks went further and found a proof that no fraction will ever hit it, not even with numbers a mile long. The diagonal of a square is a perfectly real length; you can draw it in two seconds. But it cannot be written as a ratio of whole numbers. Such numbers are called irrational, which means "without a ratio." Written as a decimal, √2 begins 1.41421356… and runs on forever without ever settling into a repeating pattern.

The story goes that the man who let this secret out was a Pythagorean named Hippasus, and that he was drowned at sea for it, thrown overboard by the brotherhood, or punished by the gods, depending on who is telling it. The tellers lived centuries afterwards, and they do not even agree about what his crime was. So: a legend. But somebody did make the discovery, and it must have landed like a thunderclap. The creed said all is number. The theorem said: not this.

🧱 The Babylonian student's round tablet gives the diagonal as 1, then 24 sixtieths, then 51 parts of 3,600, then 10 parts of 216,000. The Babylonians counted in sixties, which is why your hour still has 60 minutes. Add the pieces and you get 1.41421296. The true value starts 1.41421356. Not bad for wet clay and a reed.
🌟 Big Idea #4: The Pythagoreans' own best theorem broke the Pythagoreans' favourite belief. They could keep the belief or keep the proof, but not both. Mathematics kept the proof. When a good argument and a cherished idea collide, that is always the right way round.
★ Checkpoint 18 · A near miss
Try 1.4 as a guess for the diagonal. What is 1.4 × 1.4? (If the guess were perfect, you would get exactly 2.)
14 × 14 = 196. Now put the decimal point back: two decimal places.
★ Checkpoint 19 · Off by one
Now try the fraction 17/12. For it to equal √2, 17 × 17 would have to equal 2 × 12 × 12, which is 288. What is 17 × 17 really?
17 × 17 = 17 × 10 + 17 × 7 = 170 + 119. So close to 288, and that gap of one never closes, no matter how big the numbers get.
Chapter Ten · Everywhere · today

Put It to Work

A theorem proved is a tool earned. This one may be the most-used tool in all of mathematics. Carpenters square the corners of a house with a 3-4-5 triangle. A phone finding its position, a video game deciding whether the arrow hit the dragon, a telescope working out how far apart two stars sit on a photograph: deep inside, each of them is squaring two numbers, adding, and taking a square root.

The recipe never changes:

🧭 1. Find the right triangle, and its square corner.  2. The side across from the square corner is the hypotenuse, c.  3. Looking for the hypotenuse? Add the squares of the legs. Looking for a leg? Subtract: c² − a² = b².  4. Take the square root.

Four jobs are waiting below. For the last three you may use a calculator's √ key. The Babylonian scribes kept tables of squares beside them for exactly the same purpose, and nobody called it cheating.

★ Checkpoint 20 · Job one · the fire ladder
A fire crew's ladder is 25 m long. Its foot stands 7 m out from the wall. How high up the wall does the top reach? (Careful: the ladder is the hypotenuse. You are hunting for a leg.)
m
25 × 25 = 625 and 7 × 7 = 49. Subtract this time: 625 − 49 = 576. Now, what times itself is 576? (Try 24.)
★ Checkpoint 21 · Job two · the catcher's throw
A baseball diamond is a square with bases 90 feet apart. A runner is stealing second, and the catcher throws from home plate straight across the diamond. How long is the throw, to the nearest foot?
feet
Home, first and second make a right triangle with both legs 90. 90 × 90 = 8,100, twice: 16,200. Press √ on 16,200. (The official rule book says 127 feet 3⅜ inches. It got there the same way.)
★ Checkpoint 22 · Job three · the distance between two stars
On a star chart, one star is plotted at (−2, 1) and another at (4, 9). How far apart are they on the chart, in grid units? (Walk across, then up: those are your two legs.)
grid units
Across: from −2 to 4 is 6 steps. Up: from 1 to 9 is 8 steps. Legs 6 and 8: you have met this triangle before.
★ Checkpoint 23 · Job four · the view from orbit
The Earth's radius is about 6,371 km. The International Space Station flies about 400 km up, so it is 6,771 km from the Earth's centre. An astronaut's line of sight just grazes the Earth at the horizon, and there it meets the Earth's radius at a square corner. How far away is the astronaut's horizon, to the nearest kilometer?
km
The long side, 6,771, is the hypotenuse. 6,771² = 45,846,441 and 6,371² = 40,589,641. Subtract: 5,256,800. Then press √.
Epilogue

✦ The Proof Goes On ✦

In 1927 an American teacher named Elisha Loomis published a whole book containing nothing but proofs of this one theorem. By its second edition it held about 370 of them: sliding proofs, windmill proofs, a president's trapezoid, proofs by people famous and unknown. No other theorem in mathematics has been proved so many ways. In the same book Loomis laid down a rule: there could never be a proof using trigonometry, the mathematics of angles, because trigonometry, he said, is itself built on the Pythagorean theorem. You'd be using the thing to prove the thing.

In 2023, two high-school students from New Orleans, Calcea Johnson and Ne'Kiya Jackson, stood up at a meeting of professional mathematicians and presented a proof using trigonometry, one that carefully never leans on the theorem it is proving. It had started as a bonus question in a school math contest. Their work was published in a mathematics journal in 2024, with more new proofs added. The book said it couldn't be done. They checked anyway.

So count the chain. A scribe pressing wedges into wet clay in Babylon. Rope-stretchers in India, a commentator in China painting triangles red and yellow. A brotherhood in Italy who swore by a triangle of ten dots. Euclid in Alexandria. A congressman doodling a trapezoid. A boy in Munich who wouldn't take his uncle's word for it. Two teenagers in Louisiana. Nearly four thousand years, and the same triangle.

That is what a proof buys you. Kings, empires and whole languages have vanished since the clay tablets were written. In all that time, a² + b² = c² has not changed by a hair. It was true before anyone noticed it. It will be true when every book about it has crumbled. And it never belonged to Pythagoras, or to Babylon, or to anyone: it belongs to whoever takes the trouble to prove it again. As of today, that includes you.

The Order of the Right Angle
certifies that
Astronomer
has completed all 23 checkpoints of the tale of the secret in the squares
and is hereby granted the rank of
⭐ Master of the Hypotenuse ⭐

What you now know that most adults don't:

① In every right triangle, a² + b² = c²: the squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse. Know two sides and you can calculate the third.

② Pythagoras didn't discover it. Babylonian scribes were using it around 1800 BC, more than a thousand years before he was born. India and China found it too.

③ A rule that has worked every time you tried it is evidence. A proof covers every case at once, forever. You have now seen five: the sliding triangles, the bowstring diagram, Euclid's windmill, Garfield's trapezoid, and the schoolboy's similar triangles.

④ The diagonal of a 1 × 1 square is a number that no fraction can ever equal. The theorem broke its own discoverers' favourite belief, and they had to follow the proof anyway.

⑤ When you read the story goes, ask who wrote it down, and how long afterwards.
